items.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998
items.q: I learned that from Hugo — I learned it, he taught me

ctx.x: That’s an important lesson too, in that I know that I’ve thought sometimes when I’ve been trying to orchestrate something and I don’t have enough notes, and gee, this guy’s got nothing to play. And you’re tempted, instead of giving him a rest, to give that person a note to play. But maybe it’s not really necessary.

Oh you know, that’s a great lesson. I learned that from Hugo — I learned it, he taught me, but I don’t use it all the time, he’d say, “Ray, one of the things that you can learn, the fewer guys you use to get the desired result, and the fewer notes you use to get the desired result that you’re after, it’s always going to sound better.” And that’s a hard one. You’ve got 60 guys there, you want everybody playing all the time, you know, especially the producer, wants everybody playing all the time — “we’re paying…

Let me ask you a kind of a business question. As you became a well known arranger and producer and so forth, were you able to get better business arrangements with your record company? Did you kind of hold more power in the structure of things?
